title: AES-128 ten-pair software DFA example (DLV2003 Appendix B)

target.description: Full ten-round AES-128. Appendix B provides ten correct/faulty ciphertext pairs from an AES-128 program and recovers K10 = D014F9A8C9EE2589E13F0CC8B6630CA6; AES-128 key-schedule inversion yields the master key. This is one published worked example, not a population success experiment.

setting.key_relation: One fixed secret AES master key; no related-key oracle.
setting.key_population: All master keys in the stated attack model; no weak-key restriction is specified.
setting.plaintext_model: Each correct/faulty ciphertext pair encrypts the same possibly unknown plaintext under the same key. Repeatable paired execution is required.
assumptions: Appendix B uses an AES-128 program and lists ten paired outputs; it is not a documented physical device attack.
Faults are generated by replacing State[0] with FF just before MixColumns8. The analysis treats position and difference as unknown.
A single successful worked example does not establish a 100% population success probability.

fault_model.target: One byte of the AES encryption state, not a round-key schedule fault.
fault_model.granularity: One initial state byte; the byte error may involve several bits.
fault_model.timing: Replace one state byte just before MixColumns8, within the window after MixColumns7 and before MixColumns8.
fault_model.location: The software example faults State[0]; the recovery procedure is not given the fault position.
fault_model.value_control: For reproducibility, the generator replaces State[0] with FF; the recovery procedure assumes neither the fault value nor its position is known.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Observe a correct and a faulty output for the same input and key. A pair is not one ciphertext, and acquisition attempts are not counted.

time.reported: a few minutes (abstract; no precise setup or timing)
time.note: The abstract associates ten faulty messages with an AES-128 key recovered within a few minutes; no reproducible platform/clock or per-model benchmark is given. It is kept qualitative, not converted to seconds or other AES instances.

data.note: Appendix B explicitly lists ten paired outputs and the recovered final round key. This is the number in that software example, not an expected or worst-case acquisition budget.

memory.note: No numerical peak storage requirement is specified for the whole attack.

preprocessing.note: No separate reusable preprocessing cost is tabulated; algebraic candidate-set construction is described without a whole-attack preprocessing budget.

success.description: No numerical probability of recovering this exact key_recovery output at the recorded data budget is supplied. Necessary true-key inclusion in the modeled differential-equation candidate sets is separate from unique recovery. AppendixB reports one successful ten-pair worked example without a repeated-trial denominator; do not set population success to1.

review.scope: Exact-edition endpoint-specific success audit; preserves costs, targets, settings, existing conflicts and full-audit gates. Local author models and conditional candidate retention do not certify whole-output success.

components.description: Sections3.1–3.2: for a genuine effective nonzero byte fault and the correct location (or the enumerated union of locations), the actual affected subkey bytes satisfy the differential equation and remain among its candidates. It is not uniqueness after five/nine/ten faults or a population recovery guarantee.

evidence.locator: ACNS2003 Appendix B pp.305–306; abstract p.293 and implementation statement p.294
evidence.interpretation: The ten-pair AES-128 software example is separate from the generic analytical fault models and the proposed hardware setting. The timing headline is qualitative and applies only to AES-128.

limitations: Published software example only; the atlas has not executed or independently reproduced this attack.
No physical injection setup, general success rate, precise runtime benchmark, peak memory or total acquisition-attempt count is established.
The 00/FF hardware proposal is not evidence of a physically demonstrated attack.
